\vspace{-1.5em}
\begin{abstract}
Voters usually see a candidate's face before they learn anything about the candidate's politics. Facial impressions form within a fraction of a second and predict election outcomes, yet we know little about when voters move beyond them, and whether the conditions under which they decide govern how much political information they acquire and how they use it. We study this sequence in a preregistered three-arm online visual conjoint experiment that pairs photographs of real Colombian local candidates with short descriptions of their ideology and policy priorities. Respondents are randomly assigned for the whole interview to a nine-second decision deadline, to an effort cost of accessing information, or to an unconstrained baseline, and repeatedly choose between randomly drawn pairs of candidates. Because descriptions remain hidden until requested, the design records which candidates respondents learn about, how quickly they choose, and whom they select, separating the decision to acquire political information from the choice made with or without it. The candidate pool crosses gender, displayed ideology, facial dominance, and age, which lets us ask whether temporal and effort constraints redistribute scrutiny between women and men candidates. The primary estimands are effects of the randomized decision environment; analyses of candidate characteristics describe heterogeneity across real profile bundles rather than effects of independently randomized attributes. This working draft updates its interim estimates automatically as fieldwork proceeds.
\end{abstract}

\section{Faces arrive before facts}

Most political choices begin with a sequence so ordinary that it is easy to overlook: voters see a face before they read a platform. A visual impression arrives almost automatically, whereas learning a candidate's ideology and priorities requires time and effort. This ordering matters because judgments made from faces form after exposures as brief as 100 milliseconds and predict real election outcomes (Todorov et al. 2005; Olivola and Todorov 2010). The familiar contrast between ``faces'' and ``facts'' is therefore not merely rhetorical. It describes two sources of political judgment that become available at different speeds and at different costs.

Antonakis and Dalgas (2009) make the puzzle unusually concrete. After an imaginary voyage from Troy to Ithaca, Swiss children aged 5--13 were shown pairs of photographs from French parliamentary runoffs and asked whom they would choose as captain. Their choices predicted the actual winner with a probability of 0.71; adults' competence ratings predicted the winner with a probability of 0.72, and the child and adult response patterns were statistically indistinguishable. The participants needed no campaign knowledge, policy positions, or electoral experience to reproduce the electorate's ranking. As Antonakis and Dalgas put it, ``voters are anchored in first impressions and do not appropriately correct initial inferences'' (2009, 1183). Ballew and Todorov (2007) identify the speed of this process more directly: competence judgments after 100 or 250 milliseconds were as predictive as judgments made with unlimited exposure, and a two-second response deadline preserved predictive accuracy while instructions to deliberate lengthened response time and reduced it.

The broader literature confirms that appearance matters while leaving its mechanism open. Appearance predicts electoral success across political systems (Rosar, Klein, and Beckers 2008; Berggren, Jordahl, and Poutvaara 2010; Lawson et al. 2010), and randomly showing voters ballots with candidate photographs shortly before real elections shifts votes toward appearance-advantaged candidates (Ahler et al. 2017). Part of the observational face--vote correlation nonetheless reflects which candidates parties field in competitive races (Atkinson, Enos, and Hill 2009), and appearance-based voting is concentrated among less informed citizens exposed to television (Lenz and Lawson 2011). Photographs also work as cues in low-information elections (Banducci et al. 2008), and faces convey perceived competence, ideology, party, status, dominance, and threat rather than attractiveness alone (Mattes et al. 2010; Herrmann and Shikano 2016; Laustsen and Petersen 2016; Olivola, Tingley, and Todorov 2018).

These findings establish that faces can predict choices. They say much less about the decision process that connects a first impression to a vote: when voters stop at the face, when they seek programmatic information, and whether the circumstances in which they decide make one source of evidence dominate the other. Process-tracing research shows that voters search selectively and rely on heuristics whose usefulness depends on political expertise (Lau and Redlawsk 2001, 2006; Redlawsk 2004), and that identity and policy cues compete for weight in candidate evaluation rather than simply adding up (Jenke and Huettel 2016). Yet appearance-based voting is rarely studied as a problem of information search, and experiments on candidate choice usually hold constant the conditions under which voters decide.

We address this gap with a design that follows the decision from initial exposure to information acquisition and, ultimately, choice. Every respondent completes the same paired-candidate task with photographs and hidden political descriptions of real Colombian local candidates, while random assignment determines whether choices are made under a nine-second deadline, whether political information is costly to access, or whether neither constraint applies. Candidate-specific information requests reveal whether these constraints alter both the amount and the gendered distribution of political learning. The study thus locates inequality within a sequence---from first impression, to information acquisition, to choice---rather than only in the final vote.\footnote{The study is registered in the AEA RCT Registry, AEARCTR-0017574, version 1.3, \url{https://doi.org/10.1257/rct.17574-1.3}. IRB Approval Number 086-2025. This paper describes the protocol following pretesting, including the revised nine-second deadline and fifteen analytical tasks. The registration's sample-size fields specify 444 participants and eight tasks, whereas its abstract specifies 462 participants. The current protocol specifies 462 participants and randomizes complete profiles rather than individual attributes.}

The first contribution is to recast appearance-based voting as a problem of information acquisition and evidence integration rather than simply an association between facial impressions and electoral choice. The same observed vote can emerge from distinct processes: a voter may never consult political information, may inspect only one candidate's positions, may examine both candidates yet retain the initial visual ranking, or may use programmatic evidence to revise that ranking. Studies that observe only trait judgments or final votes cannot distinguish among these paths. By measuring candidate-specific information requests, decision time, and choice across repeated tasks, the experiment separates the decision to acquire political information from the electoral decision made in its presence or absence. Comparing a deadline, an access cost, and an unconstrained baseline then reveals whether temporal and effort constraints reduce learning altogether, make learning asymmetric across candidates, or alter choice even when average acquisition changes little.

The second contribution connects this process account to gender inequality in candidate evaluation. More extensive search about women candidates may reflect genuine openness to learning, but it may also indicate that women must supply additional evidence before voters regard them as qualified; conversely, limited search may signal either confidence or exclusion from serious consideration (Ditonto, Hamilton, and Redlawsk 2014; Bauer 2020). A gender difference in information acquisition therefore has no invariant meaning apart from the conditions under which it arises and the choices that follow it. Randomizing the decision environment supplies the relevant leverage: if the difference between women and men candidates expands, contracts, or reverses under time pressure or costly access, the experiment identifies how those constraints redistribute scrutiny across fixed profile groups, without treating candidate gender as independently randomized. Campaigns, ballot designs, and digital platforms routinely vary in the time and effort they demand from voters, so establishing whether such frictions place unequal informational burdens on women candidates links a micro-level process of political learning to broader inequalities in representation.

Colombia offers a useful source of stimuli for this question. Local elections there feature many candidates whom voters know little about, and since Law 1475 of 2011 party lists for bodies electing five or more seats must include at least 30 percent of either gender, so women and men compete on the same lists in large numbers. To prevent candidate recognition, respondents are adults who have no residential or national tie to Colombia, so their choices rely on exactly the information the interface provides. The next section develops expectations about how time and effort constraints shape the use of faces and facts. Sections~\ref{sec:design}--\ref{sec:estimation} describe the design, estimands, and estimation strategy, Section~\ref{sec:results} reports interim results that update with each data download, and Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses their implications and limits.

\section{Two frictions on political learning}
\label{sec:theory}

\subsection{Faces as default evidence}

Political information is costly to acquire, and voters economize on it by relying on whatever cues are freely available (Downs 1957; Popkin 1991). A candidate's photograph is the cheapest such cue: it requires no search and delivers an immediate impression of competence, warmth, dominance, age, and gender. Candidate evaluations are also updated on-line as information is encountered, so an early impression becomes part of a running tally even when the evidence that produced it is later forgotten (Lodge, McGraw, and Stroh 1989). Whether appearance-based competence inferences survive once substantive information is available is itself an open question (Ditonto 2018). If they do, faces are not merely a fallback for the uninformed but a default against which later information must compete. Whether programmatic information displaces that default depends first on whether voters acquire it and then on whether they have the time and inclination to integrate it.

\subsection{Time and effort as distinct constraints}

Time pressure changes how decision makers acquire and combine information. When time is scarce, people accelerate processing, filter cues, and substitute simpler noncompensatory rules for effortful integration (Payne, Bettman, and Johnson 1988; Payne, Bettman, and Luce 1996; Rieskamp and Hoffrage 2008). A deadline matters only when it binds, however: Ord\'o\~nez and Benson (1997, 122) note that ``it is possible to have time constraint but no time pressure.'' Laboratory elections show that time pressure can change voting itself, reducing strategic voting under plurality rule (Al\'os-Ferrer and Garagnani 2022). In candidate evaluation, a deadline limits two things at once: the opportunity to request information and the opportunity to weigh it against the impression already formed.

An information cost works differently. It raises the price of each additional piece of evidence while leaving time to integrate whatever is acquired. Voters facing a cost should acquire less information, but those who pay it have chosen to learn and can deliberate over what they find. The two constraints therefore make distinct predictions. Both should reduce information acquisition. A deadline should accelerate choice and may weaken the link between acquired information and the final vote, whereas an access cost should slow choice, because obtaining information takes effort, and should leave that link intact among those who acquire it. Response times are thus informative about the decision process and not only about compliance with the deadline (Spiliopoulos and Ortmann 2018).

\subsection{Gendered scrutiny}

Candidate gender can shape not only the final vote but the path by which voters learn. Voters seek more competence-related and ``compassion issue'' information about women than about men (Ditonto, Hamilton, and Redlawsk 2014), and the amount of search triggered by a woman candidate depends on partisan alignment and is strongest early in a campaign (Andersen and Ditonto 2020). Women are often required to provide stronger evidence of qualification: across survey experiments, voters applied more stringent qualification standards to women candidates (Bauer 2020), and long-standing stereotypes portray women as less agentic and tough than men (Huddy and Terkildsen 1993). A photograph makes candidate gender available before any policy text is opened, exactly the sequence in which an early cue can organize subsequent search.

The resulting penalty is neither universal nor necessarily conscious. A meta-analysis of 67 candidate-choice experiments finds that being a woman yields, on average, a modest advantage of about two percentage points (Schwarz and Coppock 2022), and experiments in Brazil find a pro-female effect of five to seven points (Aguilar, Cunow, and Desposato 2015). Conjoint evidence instead locates bias in the social roles voters expect women to occupy (Teele, Kalla, and Rosenbluth 2018). Campaign communication can activate dormant stereotypes (Bauer 2015), and the facial impressions that predict votes differ by candidate gender: competence is most predictive in men-only races and attractiveness in women-only races (Ditonto and Mattes 2018), and attractiveness weighs heavily in men's votes for women candidates (Chiao, Bowman, and Gill 2008). Bahamonde and Sarpila (2024) find a compounded penalty for working-class-looking women and weaker electoral returns to attractiveness for women than men. Eye-tracking evidence finds similar attention to stereotype-consistent and inconsistent information across candidate gender, suggesting that bias may arise from the standards applied to evidence rather than from attention alone (Jenke 2025), while think-aloud evidence shows both rapid gender heuristics and later gendered rationalizations (Rohrbach and Sch\"onhagen 2025). The empirical question is therefore not simply whether women lose. It is whether profiles of women candidates invite different patterns of information acquisition, whether constraints suppress that additional scrutiny, and whether the same evidence translates into choice differently for women and men.

\subsection{Expectations}

These arguments imply four preregistered expectations, stated formally in Section~\ref{sec:estimands}. Both constraints should reduce information acquisition (H1), and the deadline should accelerate the first selection (H2). If voters scrutinize women candidates more when learning is free, both constraints should attenuate that gendered difference (H3). Because additional scrutiny can either help women overcome stricter standards or expose them to them, constraints should change the relative selection of women and men candidates, in a direction we leave open (H4). Beyond these tests, the candidate pool allows an exploratory comparison of faces and facts. Facial dominance, which tracks the facial width-to-height ratio (fWHR; Carr\'e and McCormick 2008; Geniole et al. 2015) and whose electoral appeal varies with voters' ideology (Laustsen and Petersen 2016), is visible in every task. A candidate's ideology is visible only to respondents who open the description. If constraints shift weight from facts to faces, the selection premium for ideologically congruent candidates should shrink under a deadline or an access cost, and visible characteristics should gain influence.

\section{Research design}
\label{sec:design}

\subsection{Sample and eligibility}

The planned sample consists of 462 adults aged 18--65, balanced across men and women and allocated approximately equally across the three experimental conditions ($154$ per condition).\footnote{Participants are recruited through the survey company Borde Data (\url{https://www.bordedata.cl}).} To minimize candidate recognition and prior knowledge of Colombian politics, respondents must not be Colombian nationals, reside in Colombia, or have previously lived in Colombia. Country of residence and nationality are selected from country lists, followed by a question on previous residence in Colombia. Respondents who report a Colombian connection or decline to answer the residence-history question leave the study before the choice tasks. Eligibility screening and the baseline questionnaire precede exposure to the assigned-condition instructions. The questionnaire measures age, gender identity, occupation, education, electoral participation, political interest, frequency of political discussion, and ideological self-placement. Self-placement uses a 1--10 scale, anchored at left and right, with separate options for uncertainty, nonresponse, and identification with neither side.

A response qualifies as an eligible complete when the respondent reaches the final study screen, submits all fifteen analytical choice tasks, records a valid candidate selection in at least thirteen of them, and has no detected prohibited browser navigation. The same rule applies in all three conditions and allows at most two analytical tasks without a recorded choice. Practice-task selections do not determine completion. After the initial instructions, respondents are instructed not to refresh the browser or use browser-history navigation. Detected reloads or history navigation during subsequent instructions, practice, analytical tasks, or their follow-up questions are recorded for audit and terminate participation, classifying the response as incomplete. Detection is limited to events observable by the application and does not establish the respondent's intent. Follow-up questions are required when applicable, while responses omitted by the questionnaire's conditional structure remain undefined rather than constituting incomplete data. All substantive analyses use only responses meeting these criteria, while recruitment accounting separately reports screened-out, navigation-excluded, and other incomplete attempts (Appendix~\ref{app:collection}).

\subsection{Stimuli and repeated choice}

The stimuli are 71 real Colombian local candidates for whom a photograph and political information are available. The pool was assembled as a crossed design of real people: it combines candidate gender, displayed ideology (left, center, right), a binary facial-dominance classification, and a younger or older age group, with 2--3 candidates in each of the 24 cells. The dominance classification closely tracks the facial width-to-height ratio (median fWHR 1.95 among high- and 1.47 among low-dominance profiles). Because profiles are drawn at random from this balanced pool, the four classifications are nearly independent across displayed profiles, although each remains bundled with everything else about the real person in the photograph.

For each respondent, 40 profiles are sampled without replacement and randomly ordered. Consecutive profiles form 20 pairs, randomizing both pair composition and task order. The first five pairs are used for practice, and the remaining fifteen constitute the analytical sample. Within each task, the two candidates are assigned to left and right by an independent random permutation of the pair. No candidate therefore appears more than once for the same respondent, although candidates can appear for different respondents. Both photographs become visible together after loading. Descriptions are initially hidden and identify each candidate's ideological orientation as left, center, or right, followed by the candidate's thematic priorities. Respondents may reveal either description and revise their selection until they submit the task or the deadline expires. Information can therefore be accessed before or after an initial selection. The five practice rounds reproduce the assigned condition, including its deadline or arithmetic requirement, and are excluded from the analytical sample.

The fifteen-task analytical sequence is supported by evidence on the response quality of repeated conjoint choices. Across six online experiments involving 6,534 respondents, Bansak et al. (2018) examined thirty paired candidate choices per respondent and found only limited increases in survey satisficing; the estimated effects of candidate attributes remained broadly stable across the sequence. Paired conjoint designs also recover real-world behavioral benchmarks closely (Hainmueller, Hangartner, and Yamamoto 2015). Because the appropriate task burden also depends on the full instrument, we examine response times, information requests, nonresponse, and choice patterns across task positions to assess fatigue under the additional demands of photographic evaluation, experimental constraints, and follow-up questions.

After each analytical task with a registered selection, respondents are asked whether they would vote for the candidate they have just chosen in a real election. Those answering affirmatively identify the principal considerations underlying their choice. The eligible response options are randomized within each task, with ``Otra raz\'on'' always placed last. The questions themselves retain a fixed order. The factor list includes appearance-related considerations, while ideology and thematic priorities appear only if at least one candidate description was revealed. Perceived time pressure is measured with the same seven-point item in \armT\ and \armB, regardless of the answer to the real-election support question. Perceived effort is measured on a seven-point scale in \armC\ only when the respondent revealed information. Tasks that end without a selection skip every follow-up question.

\subsection{Experimental conditions}

Let $Z_i\in\{T,C,B\}$ denote assignment to one of three decision environments. In \armT, each task includes a visible nine-second countdown, while the candidate descriptions can be opened without an arithmetic requirement. In \armC, there is no deadline, but revealing each candidate's description requires correctly solving a simple addition problem. In \armB, neither a deadline nor an arithmetic barrier applies. Allocation occurs with equal probability at the respondent level when study sessions are initialized and remains concealed through screening and the baseline questionnaire. The candidates, number of tasks, and choice prompt are otherwise held constant. This structure distinguishes two constraints on political learning: \armT\ limits the time available to acquire and integrate information, whereas \armC\ increases the effort required to obtain it. In every condition, decision timing begins only when both photographs have loaded and decoded successfully and are revealed together. Loading time is recorded separately, and an image-loading failure prevents the task from starting until the images are available. The same nine-second deadline applies during practice and analytical tasks in \armT.\footnote{The assigned deadline is retained in browser storage when available. Participants are explicitly warned against refreshing or using browser history. Detected violations terminate participation and exclude the case from the analytical sample, while preserving previously recorded responses and the reason for termination. Stimulus readiness, deadline expiry, response preservation, and navigation handling were verified through isolated simulations and browser tests.} If the deadline expires, the current selection is submitted automatically. When no candidate has been selected, the choice remains missing.

The deadline is calibrated to the task rather than to a universal threshold for rapid judgment. A pre-test with an exploratory twenty-second deadline showed that this ceiling rarely bound: the unconstrained median task lasted 10.47 seconds. Following the relative calibration of Kocher et al. (2019), we reduced that median by 20 percent and rounded upward to nine seconds, a limit that compresses opportunities for information acquisition and comparison without making political information inaccessible. Timed respondents receive an explanation of the countdown and automatic submission, a comprehension check before practice and before the analytical sequence, and reminders after missed choices. Appendix~\ref{app:collection} details the calibration, the preparation protocol, and the resulting task durations by study version.

\subsection{Outcomes and measurement}

The primary outcomes are recorded candidate selection, whether any description is revealed, the number of descriptions revealed, time to first selection capped at a common nine-second window, and failure to register a selection within that window. Description revelation is the observed measure of information acquisition and does not establish that the text was read or understood. These candidate-specific records permit tests of gendered scrutiny. Total time from photograph display to task submission, changes in selection, and information-button presses are recorded separately. Information-acquisition measures cover the entire task, including openings after an initial selection. Terminal nonselection at the deadline is retained as a separate outcome. Post-choice measures capture whether respondents would support the selected candidate in a real election and which considerations they report using. The candidate profiles include gender, age, party affiliation, geographic constituency, electoral performance, political information, and previously measured facial characteristics. Recording the alternatives and information available in each task allows us to distinguish treatment effects on information acquisition from treatment effects on recorded selection.

\section{Potential outcomes and estimands}
\label{sec:estimands}

\subsection{Notation and common averaging distribution}

For eligible respondent $i$ in analytical task $t$, let $Z_i\in\{T,C,B\}$ denote the assigned decision environment and let $P_{it}=(C^L_{it},C^R_{it})$ denote the ordered candidate pair. For side $s\in\{L,R\}$, define $M^s_{it}(z,p)\in\{0,1\}$ as the potential indicator that the respondent reveals the political description of the candidate on side $s$ at any point before the task ends under environment $z$ and pair $p$. This measures access to the text, without establishing that it was read or understood. Respondents may reveal information after an initial selection and revise that selection before submission. Aggregate information acquisition is defined as
\[
K_{it}(z,p)=M^L_{it}(z,p)+M^R_{it}(z,p),\quad
A_{it}(z,p)=\mathbf 1\{K_{it}(z,p)\geq 1\},\quad
X_{it}(z,p)=\mathbf 1\{K_{it}(z,p)=2\}.
\]
Thus, $K$ is the number of descriptions revealed, $A$ indicates access to at least one description, and $X$ indicates access to both descriptions.

Let $T^*_{it}(z,p)$ denote seconds from the simultaneous display of both fully loaded photographs to the first candidate selection, with $T^*=\infty$ if no selection occurs. To place all conditions on a common observation window, define capped selection latency $D^{9}_{it}(z,p)=\min\{T^*_{it}(z,p),9\}$ and slow or absent selection $S^{9}_{it}(z,p)=\mathbf 1\{T^*_{it}(z,p)>9\}$. If no selection occurs within nine seconds, $D^{9}=9$ and $S^{9}=1$. This common analytical window does not impose a deadline on the baseline or arithmetic-cost conditions, whose uncapped response times remain recorded. The full task duration, measured from photograph display to submission, is recorded separately and can include information acquisition and revisions after the first selection. Loading time precedes both measures. Let $Q_{it}(z,p)$ indicate that a task terminates at the deadline without any candidate selection. This outcome is possible under \armT; the other conditions require a selection before submission. Reaching the deadline after selecting a candidate preserves the current selection and gives $Q=0$. Thus, $S^{9}$ measures failure to select within the common window, while $Q$ identifies termination without a candidate response.

Candidate choice is defined without privileging the randomized left position. Let $V_{it}(z,p)$ denote the candidate selected when the task ends; $V=\varnothing$ denotes a missing candidate response when $Q=1$. For each displayed side, define the registered-selection event
\[
Y^s_{it}(z,p)=\mathbf 1\{V_{it}(z,p)=C^s_{it}\}.
\]
When a candidate response is recorded, $Y^L_{it}+Y^R_{it}=1$; when $Q_{it}=1$, both derived event indicators equal zero, while the candidate response itself remains missing. This definition neither imputes a vote nor assigns an unobserved preference to a respondent who made no selection. In the full eligible randomized population, its expectation is the probability that a displayed profile receives a registered selection under the assigned environment. Effects on this outcome can reflect both changes in which candidate is selected and changes in whether any selection is completed.

Unless otherwise stated, the causal estimands below weight eligible respondents and the fifteen analytical tasks equally and average over the randomized candidate draw, pairing, task order, and left-right assignment. Practice tasks are excluded. Comparisons between $z\in\{T,C\}$ and \armB\ define respondent-level intention-to-treat targets. The reported estimates are restricted to completed responses and must be distinguished from these full-population targets, as detailed in the estimation strategy.

\subsection{Effects of the decision environment}

For each task-level outcome $R\in\{A,K,X,D^{9},S^{9}\}$, define
\[
\tau^R_{zB}=\E\!\left[R_{it}(z,P_{it})-R_{it}(B,P_{it})\right],
\qquad z\in\{T,C\}.
\]
The terminal-timeout effect is defined separately as $\tau^Q_{TB}=\E[Q_{it}(T,P_{it})-Q_{it}(B,P_{it})]$ because forced task termination exists only in \armT. These estimands capture how temporal scarcity and information cost change information acquisition, decision speed, and response completion. Information acquisition is also a potential mediator of candidate choice. Because it occurs after treatment, models that condition choice on realized information acquisition do not identify a controlled or natural direct effect without additional assumptions; mediation analyses are therefore interpreted cautiously and do not carry a direct-effect interpretation.

Randomized pairing and position also identify side-neutral profile-selection probabilities. For complete candidate profile $c$, define
\[
\theta_c(z)=\E\!\left[Y^s_{it}(z,P_{it})\mid C^s_{it}=c\right],\qquad
\Delta_c(z)=\theta_c(z)-\theta_c(B).
\]
The expectation averages over respondents, tasks, randomized rivals, and side. $\Delta_c(z)$ is the causal effect of the decision environment on the probability that profile $c$ is selected when displayed. Contrasts $\theta_c(z)-\theta_{c'}(z)$ compare randomly assigned complete profiles under the same environment. They do not isolate gender, ideology, party, or facial characteristics because those attributes remain bundled within each observed candidate.

\subsection{Gendered information acquisition and choice}

Let $G(c)=1$ denote a profile coded as a woman. For $R\in\{M,Y\}$, define the candidate-level mean, gender-indexed contrast, and treatment-induced change as
\[
\mu^R_g(z)=\E\!\left[R^s_{it}(z,P_{it})\mid G(C^s_{it})=g\right],\quad
\Gamma_R(z)=\mu^R_1(z)-\mu^R_0(z),\quad
\Psi_R(z)=\Gamma_R(z)-\Gamma_R(B).
\]
$\Gamma_M(z)$ compares the probability of consulting political information about women and men candidates, while $\Gamma_Y(z)$ compares their probability of selection. The corresponding $\Psi_M(z)$ and $\Psi_Y(z)$ estimands identify how random assignment to a constrained decision environment changes each gender-indexed contrast. Candidate gender is not independently randomized, so $\Gamma_M(z)$ and $\Gamma_Y(z)$ compare complete profiles grouped by gender and are not causal effects of gender. The causal interpretation of $\Psi_M(z)$ and $\Psi_Y(z)$ is limited to the effect of the randomized environment on those fixed profile-group differences.

\subsection{Hypotheses and analytical priorities}

The \textbf{primary process family} consists of $\tau^A_{zB}$, $\tau^K_{zB}$, $\tau^{D^{9}}_{zB}$, and $\tau^{S^{9}}_{zB}$ for $z\in\{T,C\}$. The \textbf{primary gender-interaction family} consists of $\Psi_M(T)$, $\Psi_M(C)$, $\Psi_Y(T)$, and $\Psi_Y(C)$. The baseline contrasts $\Gamma_M(B)$ and $\Gamma_Y(B)$ form a separate descriptive family because candidate gender is not independently assigned. Hypothesis tests are two-sided even where theory implies a direction. Their empirical counterparts are estimated among completed responses, so the causal status of the target estimands does not by itself establish a causal interpretation for the reported contrasts.

We expect both constrained conditions to reduce any information acquisition and the number of descriptions consulted, $\tau^A_{zB}<0$ and $\tau^K_{zB}<0$ (H1). We also expect \armT\ to reduce capped selection latency, $\tau^{D^{9}}_{TB}<0$, while effects on $S^{9}$ and the timing effects of \armC\ are tested without directional restrictions (H2). Under \armB, we expect respondents to consult information more often for profiles of women candidates, $\Gamma_M(B)>0$, and both constraints to attenuate this difference, $\Psi_M(T)<0$ and $\Psi_M(C)<0$ (H3). Finally, we expect $\Psi_Y(T)$ and $\Psi_Y(C)$ to differ from zero, with their signs left open because prior work implies both potential penalties and advantages for women candidates (H4).

\textbf{Additional estimands} include acquisition of both descriptions $X$, terminal timeout $Q$, full task duration, profile-specific $\theta_c(z)$ and $\Delta_c(z)$, the real-election support item, self-reported time pressure and information cost, ideological congruence, associations between choice and other candidate characteristics, and moderation by respondent gender or political sophistication. \textbf{Additional analyses} examine mediation through information acquisition, models conditioned on realized information acquisition or completed choice, high-dimensional profile interactions, decision-factor responses, and subgroup variation. Because these analyses require further assumptions or extend beyond the central hypotheses, they are interpreted separately from the primary tests.

\subsection{Timeout and missing-data rules}

For respondents meeting the response-completion criteria, all descriptions revealed before a task terminates contribute to $M^s$, $A$, $K$, and $X$, including when no candidate is selected. A task with no selection within nine seconds receives $D^{9}=9$ and $S^{9}=1$. If the \armT\ task terminates without a selection, $Q=1$, the recorded candidate response remains missing, the derived registered-selection indicators satisfy $Y^L=Y^R=0$, and every follow-up question is skipped. These undefined follow-up responses will not be imputed. If a selection has already occurred when the deadline expires, the current candidate response is retained, $Q=0$, and the usual follow-up questions are shown. Up to two missing analytical choices are permitted within a completed response, and their associated information and timing outcomes remain in the analysis. Participation ends when a third analytical task is submitted without a valid selection, because the minimum response requirement can no longer be met. These respondents, and those who otherwise do not finish the study, are excluded from substantive analyses but remain in recruitment accounting, with their previously recorded responses preserved. Withdrawal or abandonment before task submission is not recoded as a timeout. No missing candidate choice or undefined follow-up response will be imputed.

\section{Estimation strategy}
\label{sec:estimation}

All substantive analyses are restricted to eligible completed responses as defined above. Each retained respondent contributes all fifteen analytical tasks, including up to two tasks without a registered candidate selection. Let $H_i=1$ indicate that respondent $i$ meets the observed completion criteria. For a task-level outcome $R$, the estimable condition contrast is
\[
\delta^R_{zB}=\E[R_{it}\mid Z_i=z,H_i=1]-\E[R_{it}\mid Z_i=B,H_i=1].
\]
Because the decision environment may affect reaching the final screen, recording at least thirteen choices, or detected browser navigation, conditioning on $H_i=1$ can select different respondents across conditions. Consequently, $\delta^R_{zB}$ need not equal the full-population intention-to-treat effect $\tau^R_{zB}$, even under randomized assignment. The reported contrasts are therefore interpreted as completion-conditioned comparisons rather than automatically as causal effects for all eligible randomized respondents. Screening, final-screen arrival, navigation-related exclusions, and other incomplete responses are reported separately to make this selection transparent. The candidate-level contrasts $\Gamma_R(z)$ and $\Psi_R(z)$ are estimated on the same completion-conditioned footing.

Every primary estimand is estimated in two ways. The main estimators are the preregistered differences: differences in condition means for the process outcomes and differences in women-minus-men gaps for the candidate-level outcomes. They rely only on random assignment and involve no specification choices. Complementary regression-adjusted models, introduced during fieldwork after the preregistration, re-estimate the same contrasts while adjusting for information fixed before the assigned condition was revealed. Under random assignment, such adjustment leaves the target contrast unchanged and can remove outcome variation that would otherwise appear as sampling noise (Freedman 2008; Lin 2013). Comparing the two estimators also shows how much a result depends on chance imbalance in pretreatment characteristics. Binary outcomes enter every linear model as linear probability models, so coefficients are differences in probabilities on the scale of the estimands (Angrist and Pischke 2009).

\subsection{Main estimators: preregistered differences}

For outcome $R\in\{A,K,D^{9},S^{9}\}$ of respondent $i$ in task $t$, the difference in condition means is the ordinary least squares coefficient $\delta^R_{zB}$ in
\begin{equation}
R_{it}=\alpha+\sum_{z\in\{T,C\}}\delta^R_{zB}\,D^z_i+\varepsilon_{it},
\label{eq:dim}
\end{equation}
where $D^z_i=\mathbf 1\{Z_i=z\}$, so $\alpha$ is the \armB\ mean. Replacing $\alpha$ with a \armB\ indicator gives the condition means in Figure~\ref{fig:process}A, and the same specification applied to reported hurry in \armB\ and \armT\ gives the manipulation check in Appendix~\ref{app:collection}. Standard errors are clustered by respondent, the level of assignment (Abadie et al. 2023), with Student-$t$ critical values on the number of respondents minus one degrees of freedom.

For the candidate-level outcomes $R\in\{M,Y\}$, each task contributes one observation per displayed candidate. With $j$ indexing candidates and $W_j=G(j)$ indicating a woman, the preregistered linear probability model is
\begin{equation}
R_{itj}=\alpha+\sum_{z\in\{T,C\}}\beta_z\,D^z_i+\gamma\,W_j+\sum_{z\in\{T,C\}}\psi_z\,D^z_iW_j+\pi\,\mathit{Side}_{itj}+\lambda_t+u_{itj},
\label{eq:lpm}
\end{equation}
where $\mathit{Side}_{itj}$ marks the randomized right-hand position and $\lambda_t$ are task-position fixed effects. The coefficient $\gamma$ estimates the baseline gap $\Gamma_R(B)$, $\gamma+\psi_z$ estimates $\Gamma_R(z)$, and $\psi_z$ estimates $\Psi_R(z)$. Side and task position are randomized independently of candidate gender and condition, so these coefficients remain differences in gaps between condition means. Uncertainty uses two-way clustering by respondent and candidate (Cameron, Gelbach, and Miller 2011), with critical values on the smaller cluster count minus one degrees of freedom.

\subsection{Complementary regression-adjusted models}

For the process outcomes, the regression-adjusted model is
\begin{equation}
R_{it}=\alpha+\sum_{z\in\{T,C\}}\delta^R_{zB}\,D^z_i+\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i'\boldsymbol{\beta}+\sum_{z\in\{T,C\}}D^z_i\,\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i'\boldsymbol{\beta}_z+\varepsilon_{it},
\label{eq:lin}
\end{equation}
where $\tilde{\mathbf{x}}_i=\mathbf{x}_i-\bar{\mathbf{x}}$ collects four pretreatment covariates, centered at their means in the analytical sample: age in decades, an indicator for women, an indicator for tertiary education, and political interest on the 1--7 scale. Equation~\eqref{eq:lin} is the fully interacted estimator of Lin (2013). Interacting the centered covariates with each condition is equivalent to fitting a separate regression in each condition and comparing the fitted means at the common covariate average, so the coefficients on $D^z_i$ estimate the same contrasts as Equation~\eqref{eq:dim}. Under random assignment, this estimator is consistent whether or not the conditional mean is linear, and it is asymptotically at least as precise as the difference in means when effects are heterogeneous, allocation is unequal, or there are more than two conditions (Lin 2013; Negi and Wooldridge 2021; Ye et al. 2023). Additive adjustment without the interactions lacks this guarantee under unequal allocation (Freedman 2008), which applies during fieldwork.

The covariates come from the baseline questionnaire, which precedes the assigned instructions. The model excludes information acquisition, response times, reported hurry, and arithmetic success: these are consequences of assignment, and conditioning on them would bias the contrasts (Montgomery, Nyhan, and Torres 2018). Political interest and education index the political sophistication that shapes information search (Lau and Redlawsk 2006), and age and gender are standard predictors of response behavior. The list is deliberately short, because each covariate adds three parameters. Assignment varies only across respondents, and every respondent contributes all fifteen tasks, so Equation~\eqref{eq:lin} is equivalent to a respondent-level regression of within-respondent outcome means (Su and Ding 2021). For the same reason, task-position indicators would be orthogonal to every regressor and would leave the estimates unchanged, so they are omitted: precision gains for this family can come only from respondent characteristics. Inference follows Equation~\eqref{eq:dim}.

For the candidate-level outcomes, the regression-adjusted model of the gender interactions is
\begin{equation}
R_{itj}=\alpha_i+\eta_j+\sum_{z\in\{T,C\}}\psi_z\,D^z_iW_j+\sum_{z\in\{B,T,C\}}\kappa_z\,D^z_i\,\mathit{Cong}_{ij}+\omega\,W_j\tilde F_i+\pi\,\mathit{Side}_{itj}+\lambda_t+u_{itj},
\label{eq:psi}
\end{equation}
where $\alpha_i$ and $\eta_j$ are respondent and candidate fixed effects and $D^B_i=\mathbf 1\{Z_i=B\}$. The indicator $\mathit{Cong}_{ij}$ equals one when the candidate's displayed ideology matches the respondent's pretreatment self-placement (left 1--4, center 5--6, right 7--10) and zero otherwise, including for respondents without a numeric placement, and $\tilde F_i$ is the centered indicator for women respondents. Respondent effects absorb each respondent's general propensity to open descriptions or register selections, the assigned condition, and every respondent characteristic. Candidate effects absorb everything that is fixed about a real profile, including its photograph, party, biography, and gender. In Equation~\eqref{eq:psi}, $\psi_z$ is therefore identified from how the within-respondent difference between women and men changes across randomly assigned environments for the same real candidates, so it does not depend on which profiles happened to be drawn more often in one condition. Conditions are randomized across respondents and profiles are drawn independently of the condition, so the fixed effects and pretreatment terms are unrelated to assignment and leave the contrast unchanged. Ideological congruence is the strongest observed predictor of selection (Section~\ref{sec:faces-facts}) and may matter differently in each environment. The respondent-by-candidate gender term absorbs same-gender affinity (Sanbonmatsu 2002).

Because candidate gender is constant within a profile, candidate fixed effects also absorb the gender gaps. The regression-adjusted gaps within each condition therefore come from the same specification without $\eta_j$, with candidate gender interacted with every condition:
\begin{equation}
R_{itj}=\alpha_i+\sum_{z\in\{B,T,C\}}\gamma_z\,D^z_iW_j+\sum_{z\in\{B,T,C\}}\kappa_z\,D^z_i\,\mathit{Cong}_{ij}+\omega\,W_j\tilde F_i+\pi\,\mathit{Side}_{itj}+\lambda_t+u_{itj}.
\label{eq:gamma}
\end{equation}
Here $\gamma_z$ estimates $\Gamma_R(z)$ as a within-respondent women-minus-men difference. Congruence depends on displayed ideology, but the pool crosses gender with ideology, so the two are nearly orthogonal across appearances (correlation 0.03), and the term absorbs outcome variance rather than redefining the comparison. Inference for Equations~\eqref{eq:psi} and~\eqref{eq:gamma} follows Equation~\eqref{eq:lpm}.

\subsection{Reading the two estimators together}

Within the primary process and gender-interaction families, two-sided $p$-values are adjusted by Holm's sequential procedure, separately for each estimator; the two baseline gender contrasts constitute a third, descriptive multiplicity family. Table~\ref{tab:primary} reports both estimators for every primary test, the ratio of their standard errors, and which of them reject zero at the Holm-adjusted 5 percent level. Appendix Tables~\ref{tab:process-models} and~\ref{tab:candidate-models} report the fitted models. Interpretation rests on both estimators. A result is described as robust when both reject zero with the same sign. When only the preregistered difference rejects zero, the result holds under the main test but depends on the estimator. When only the regression-adjusted model rejects zero, the result is suggestive, because the main test does not support it. When neither rejects zero, the estimand is not distinguishable from zero at the current sample size, and the intervals show which magnitudes remain plausible. Where the two point estimates differ, the gap reflects chance imbalance in the pretreatment covariates (Table~\ref{tab:variables}, panel A), which the adjustment removes.

\subsection{Exploratory analyses}

Exploratory analyses describe which candidate characteristics are associated with registered selection in each decision environment. Let $\mathbf{a}_j$ collect indicators for a woman, left- and right-identified displayed ideology (center is the reference), high facial dominance, and the older age group. The joint linear probability model is
\begin{equation}
Y_{itj}=\alpha+\sum_{z\in\{T,C\}}\beta_z\,D^z_i+\sum_{z\in\{B,T,C\}}D^z_i\,\mathbf{a}_j'\boldsymbol{\phi}_z+\pi\,\mathit{Side}_{itj}+\lambda_t+u_{itj},
\label{eq:traits}
\end{equation}
so the elements of $\boldsymbol{\phi}_z$ are within-condition contrasts: women versus men, left- and right-identified versus centrist profiles, high versus low dominance, and older versus younger profiles. Among respondents with a numeric self-placement, the congruence model is
\begin{equation}
Y_{itj}=\alpha+\sum_{z\in\{T,C\}}\beta_z\,D^z_i+\sum_{z\in\{B,T,C\}}\kappa_z\,D^z_i\,\mathit{Cong}_{ij}+\pi\,\mathit{Side}_{itj}+\lambda_t+u_{itj},
\label{eq:congruence}
\end{equation}
where $\kappa_z$ is the selection premium for ideologically congruent profiles in condition $z$. Because profiles are real bundles, these are adjusted associations across observed profiles rather than causal effects of independently assigned attributes (Hainmueller, Hopkins, and Yamamoto 2014; Abramson, Ko\c{c}ak, and Magazinnik 2022). Comparing a within-condition contrast across conditions compares gaps between levels rather than the overall favorability of any level, and for multi-level classifications such comparisons depend on the reference category, so we read them as changes in relative selection (Leeper, Hobolt, and Tilley 2020). Neither model conditions on whether respondents opened political information. Both use two-way clustering by respondent and candidate and unadjusted tests that remain separate from the primary families.

Profile-specific selection probabilities are estimated by the share of a profile's appearances that end in its selection:
\begin{equation}
\hat\theta_c(z)=\frac{\sum_{i,t,s}\mathbf 1\{Z_i=z,\,C^s_{it}=c\}\,Y^s_{it}}{\sum_{i,t,s}\mathbf 1\{Z_i=z,\,C^s_{it}=c\}},\qquad
\hat\Delta_c(z)=\hat\theta_c(z)-\hat\theta_c(B).
\label{eq:theta}
\end{equation}
Side and rival are randomized, so these shares are side-neutral, but they condition on completed responses and are not attribute-level average marginal component effects. Stated decision factors are summarized as shares of eligible tasks by condition,
\begin{equation}
\hat\rho_k(z)=\frac{\sum_{i,t}\mathbf 1\{Z_i=z\}\,E_{itk}\,N_{itk}}{\sum_{i,t}\mathbf 1\{Z_i=z\}\,E_{itk}},
\label{eq:reasons}
\end{equation}
where $E_{itk}$ indicates that factor $k$ was offered and $N_{itk}$ that it was named, with intervals clustered by respondent. Because the factors are asked only after a registered selection and a positive real-election answer, these shares describe reasons among those responses rather than effects of the environment. Finally, Appendix Figure~\ref{fig:respondent-scrutiny} describes information acquisition by respondent gender with a saturated logit,
\begin{equation}
\operatorname{logit}\Pr(M_{itj}=1)=\mu_{Z_i,\,W_j,\,F_i},
\label{eq:scrutiny}
\end{equation}
with one parameter for each combination of condition, candidate gender, and respondent gender $F_i$, so that its fitted probabilities equal the observed cell shares; intervals use two-way clustering on the logit scale.

% Results stay out of the paper until all treatment arms are represented.

\section{Interim results}
\label{sec:results}

\noindent\textit{Status of fieldwork.} This section is regenerated from the most recent export (20 November 2026). It uses 67 eligible completed responses---27 in \armB, 22 in \armT, and 18 in \armC---or 15 percent of the planned 462. They contribute 1,005 analytical tasks and 2,010 candidate appearances. These are interim monitoring estimates: they do not define a significance-based stopping rule, and the preregistered analysis of the complete sample will supersede them. Recruitment, sample composition, and implementation checks are in Appendix~\ref{app:collection}.

Table~\ref{tab:variables} describes every variable used in the analysis at the level at which it is measured, overall and by condition. Panel C doubles as a randomization check on the displayed profiles, and panel A shows how far the conditions differ by chance in the pretreatment covariates that enter Equation~\eqref{eq:lin}. Table~\ref{tab:primary} reports every preregistered primary test: the main preregistered difference, the complementary regression-adjusted estimate, and which of the two reject zero after Holm correction. Figures~\ref{fig:process}--\ref{fig:profiles} display the corresponding estimands. Of the 14 primary tests, 2 ($\tau^{D^{9}}_{TB}$, $\tau^{S^{9}}_{TB}$) reject zero under both estimators, none only under the preregistered differences, none only under the regression-adjusted models, and 12 under neither. The ratio of regression-adjusted to preregistered standard errors has a median of 0.94 (range 0.78--1.06; smaller in 7 of 8) in the process family and 0.99 (range 0.75--1.06; smaller in 2 of 4) in the gender-interaction family; ratios below one are precision gains from adjustment. These gains are bounded by the design: the process conditions vary only across respondents, so only respondent characteristics can absorb noise, and the preregistered gender estimator already compares women and men within respondents.

\subsection{Information acquisition and decision speed}

Figure~\ref{fig:process} reports the primary process outcomes. Under \armB, respondents opened at least one description in 90.9 percent of tasks and opened 1.75 of the two descriptions on average. Relative to \armB, the difference in the probability of opening any description ($\tau^A_{zB}$) was $-$6.9 percentage points (95\% CI $-$23.9 to 10.0; Holm-adjusted $p=0.835$) under \armT\ and $-$18.6 percentage points (95\% CI $-$42.3 to 5.0; Holm-adjusted $p=0.602$) under \armC; the regression-adjusted estimates were $-$17.1 (Holm-adjusted $p=0.181$) and $-$27.1 (Holm-adjusted $p=0.098$). The difference in the number of descriptions opened ($\tau^K_{zB}$) was $-$0.14 (95\% CI $-$0.49 to 0.21; Holm-adjusted $p=0.835$) under \armT\ and $-$0.35 (95\% CI $-$0.82 to 0.11; Holm-adjusted $p=0.602$) under \armC, against regression-adjusted estimates of $-$0.39 (Holm-adjusted $p=0.112$) and $-$0.54 (Holm-adjusted $p=0.098$). Reading the two estimators together, for $\tau^{A}_{zB}$, neither estimator rejects zero under either constraint, and for $\tau^{K}_{zB}$, neither estimator rejects zero under either constraint.

The theory expects the two constraints to act differently on timing: a deadline should speed the first selection, whereas an access cost should slow it, because information must be earned before it is used. Relative to \armB, the difference in capped time to first selection ($\tau^{D^{9}}_{zB}$) was $-$1.76 seconds (95\% CI $-$2.80 to $-$0.73; Holm-adjusted $p=0.008$) under \armT\ and 1.04 seconds (95\% CI $-$0.28 to 2.36; Holm-adjusted $p=0.602$) under \armC. The share of tasks without a selection within nine seconds ($\tau^{S^{9}}_{zB}$) changed by $-$39.2 percentage points (95\% CI $-$54.4 to $-$24.0; Holm-adjusted $p<0.001$) under \armT\ and 28.4 percentage points (95\% CI 4.3 to 52.5; Holm-adjusted $p=0.131$) under \armC. The regression-adjusted estimates were $-$2.00 seconds (Holm-adjusted $p<0.001$) and 0.54 seconds (Holm-adjusted $p=0.387$) for $\tau^{D^{9}}_{zB}$, and $-$43.5 percentage points (Holm-adjusted $p<0.001$) and 20.4 percentage points (Holm-adjusted $p=0.181$) for $\tau^{S^{9}}_{zB}$. After Holm correction, for $\tau^{D^{9}}_{zB}$, both estimators reject zero under \armT\ and neither estimator rejects zero under \armC, and for $\tau^{S^{9}}_{zB}$, both estimators reject zero under \armT\ and neither estimator rejects zero under \armC. Figure~\ref{fig:process}B shows each contrast under both estimators.

\subsection{Gendered scrutiny and selection}

Figure~\ref{fig:gender} turns to the candidate-level estimands. Under \armB, the women-minus-men difference in the probability of opening a candidate's description was $\Gamma_M(B)=$ 1.6 percentage points (95\% CI $-$0.7 to 4.0; Holm-adjusted $p=0.356$), and 0.8 points (Holm-adjusted $p=0.554$) as a within-respondent difference from Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma}; H3 anticipates a positive gap. The change in this gap was $\Psi_M(T)=$ $-$4.6 points (95\% CI $-$10.0 to 0.7; Holm-adjusted $p=0.264$) under \armT\ and $\Psi_M(C)=$ $-$1.8 points (95\% CI $-$6.4 to 2.8; Holm-adjusted $p=0.436$) under \armC. Holding the compared candidates fixed with respondent and candidate fixed effects, the regression-adjusted changes were 0.0 points (Holm-adjusted $p=1.000$) and $-$0.1 points (Holm-adjusted $p=1.000$).

For selection, the baseline gap was $\Gamma_Y(B)=$ $-$4.7 percentage points (95\% CI $-$13.5 to 4.1; Holm-adjusted $p=0.356$), and $-$5.0 points (Holm-adjusted $p=0.520$) after adjustment. Relative to that gap, the women-minus-men difference in selection changed by $\Psi_Y(T)=$ 13.9 points (95\% CI 0.5 to 27.3; Holm-adjusted $p=0.166$) under \armT\ and $\Psi_Y(C)=$ 11.5 points (95\% CI $-$4.2 to 27.1; Holm-adjusted $p=0.296$) under \armC, with regression-adjusted estimates of 12.5 points (Holm-adjusted $p=0.279$) and 9.0 points (Holm-adjusted $p=0.706$). After Holm correction, for $\Psi_M(z)$, neither estimator rejects zero under either constraint, and for $\Psi_Y(z)$, neither estimator rejects zero under either constraint. Within the constrained environments, the selection gap was 9.3 points (95\% CI $-$1.8 to 20.3; $p=0.098$) under \armT\ and 6.8 points (95\% CI $-$6.6 to 20.2; $p=0.313$) under \armC. These contrasts compare naturally occurring profiles of women and men; they show how the constraints redistribute selection between the two groups of real candidates, not the effect of changing a candidate's gender.

\subsection{Faces or facts?}
\label{sec:faces-facts}

Figure~\ref{fig:traits} asks which characteristics of the displayed profiles are associated with selection in each environment. The ideology of a candidate is a fact that respondents see only after opening a description, whereas gender, age, and facial dominance are visible in the photograph. The selection premium for ideologically congruent candidates---the difference in selection probability between profiles whose displayed ideology matched the respondent's self-placement and those that did not---was 30.0 percentage points (95\% CI 18.1 to 41.9; $p<0.001$) under \armB, 28.1 points (95\% CI 17.6 to 38.7; $p<0.001$) under \armT, and 23.2 points (95\% CI 11.3 to 35.2; $p<0.001$) under \armC. The corresponding association for high- versus low-dominance faces was 0.7 points (95\% CI $-$6.5 to 7.8; $p=0.855$) under \armB, 6.4 points (95\% CI $-$1.6 to 14.4; $p=0.115$) under \armT, and $-$5.0 points (95\% CI $-$12.3 to 2.3; $p=0.179$) under \armC.

Respondents' own accounts offer a complementary view. Among tasks in which respondents would support their chosen candidate in a real election, the candidate's appearance or first impression was cited in 21 percent of \armB\ tasks, 20 percent of \armT\ tasks, and 25 percent of \armC\ tasks (Figure~\ref{fig:reasons}). Where a description had been opened, the candidate's ideology was cited in 48, 66, and 60 percent of tasks, and policy priorities in 69, 59, and 79 percent, respectively. Stated reasons are post-choice self-reports and cannot by themselves establish which evidence drove a decision, but they show how respondents themselves weigh faces and facts.

\subsection{Profile-level choices}

Finally, Figure~\ref{fig:profiles} compares the selection probability of each real profile under each constraint with its probability under \armB, the estimands $\theta_c(z)$ and $\Delta_c(z)$. If the same candidates win regardless of how voters decide, points cluster around the diagonal; if constraints reshuffle the ranking, they scatter away from it. The current correlation between $\hat\theta_c(T)$ and $\hat\theta_c(B)$ is $-$0.03, and between $\hat\theta_c(C)$ and $\hat\theta_c(B)$ it is 0.00. With a median of 8 appearances per profile and constrained condition, these correlations are attenuated by sampling noise and will become informative only as fieldwork accumulates.

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

The experiment examines whether randomized constraints alter political information acquisition, candidate choice, and the scrutiny applied to women candidates. Its central design choice is to treat appearance-based voting as the outcome of a search process: respondents always see the faces, and the decision environment governs how costly it is to go beyond them. This makes it possible to ask not only whether faces matter but when voters stop at them. The interim estimates in Section~\ref{sec:results} illustrate how the evidence will accumulate. They show how much programmatic information respondents request when it is free, how a binding deadline and an access cost change the timing of choice, and how the women-minus-men differences in search and selection move across environments. The congruence estimates indicate how strongly respondents use a candidate's ideology once they can see it, which determines how consequential the access constraints are for programmatic voting. Reading the preregistered differences together with the regression-adjusted models shows which of these patterns survive adjustment for chance imbalance in respondent characteristics. The interim sample is a fraction of the planned one, however, and the preregistered tests of the complete sample will determine which patterns are robust.

Several limits qualify the interpretation. First, the reported comparisons are restricted to eligible completed responses, so their causal interpretation depends on assumptions about completion-related selection; Appendix~\ref{app:collection} documents attrition by stage. Second, gender, ideology, party, and facial characteristics remain bundled within observed candidates. The crossed construction of the candidate pool makes the main classifications nearly independent, but gender-indexed comparisons still capture heterogeneity across naturally occurring profiles rather than isolated attribute effects. Third, opening a description shows that information was accessed, not that it was read, understood, or believed, and stated reasons are self-reports. Fourth, respondents are deliberately unfamiliar with Colombian politics. This removes recognition and partisan attachment, approximating voters who meet unfamiliar local candidates with little prior information, but it means that the magnitudes should not be read as estimates for Colombian voters. Within these limits, combining randomized decision environments, repeated choices, and behavioral measures of political learning connects appearance-based judgment to the acquisition and use of substantive information.

\section{Data collection and implementation}
\label{app:collection}

\subsection{Deadline calibration}

The time-pressure manipulation is calibrated to the demands of the decision task rather than to a universal threshold for rapid judgment. A consequential deadline must restrict the time respondents would otherwise use to acquire and evaluate information (Ord\'o\~nez and Benson 1997), and temporal constraints can induce faster processing, more selective information search, and changes in decision strategy (Payne, Bettman, and Johnson 1988). Although Ballew and Todorov (2007) elicited electorally predictive competence judgments under a two-second deadline, their task involved photographs alone. The present task additionally permits respondents to reveal and compare political descriptions. Across the available candidate pairs, these descriptions contain a median of 28 words in total. Brysbaert's (2019) estimated Spanish silent-reading rate of 278 words per minute implies approximately six seconds of uninterrupted reading, before allowing for information access, comparison, and candidate selection (see also Caballero Germain et al. 2021 on remotely measured reading speed among Spanish-speaking university students). This calculation provides context rather than a minimum comprehension time. Keystroke-level models assign standard operator times to pointing and clicking (Card, Moran, and Newell 1980; Sauro 2009), but cursor movement and target selection depend on interface geometry and input devices, making fixed allowances per click inappropriate (MacKenzie 1992). The relevant benchmark is consequently respondents' observed performance on the experimental task itself.

The pre-test evaluated an exploratory twenty-second deadline against an unconstrained baseline. It comprised 30 eligible completed responses, contributing 450 observations across 15 analytical tasks per respondent. Pooled mean task duration was 13.68 seconds (SD 14.64; 13 respondents, 195 tasks) in the unconstrained condition and 9.99 seconds (SD 4.28; 10 respondents, 150 tasks) under the exploratory 20-second deadline; the arithmetic-cost condition contributed the remaining 7 respondents and 105 tasks. The unconstrained median was 10.47 seconds (interquartile range 6.43--15.27), and only 15.9 percent of unconstrained tasks (31 of 195) lasted longer than 20 seconds. The exploratory ceiling therefore frequently exceeded the time respondents used without a deadline. To impose a more binding restriction, we adapt the calibration principle of Kocher et al. (2019, 220--221), whose deadlines represented ``a 20\% reduction of the median decision times in the absence of constraints.'' Their restrictions applied to blocks of choices rather than individual tasks, so we adopt the relative principle rather than the implementation. Applying that reduction to the unconstrained median yields 8.38 seconds, rounded upward to nine seconds, approximately 14 percent below the observed median. Rounding upward retains a modest margin for information access and response registration while keeping the deadline below typical unconstrained task duration. Although nine seconds exceeds the unconstrained median time to first selection of 8.39 seconds, it remains below the typical time used to complete the full task. Its effectiveness is assessed jointly through reported hurry, information acquisition, and nonselection at the deadline (Table~\ref{tab:implementation}), rather than inferred from mechanically shortened durations alone. Figure~\ref{fig:task-duration-completes} compares task durations in the pre-test and the current protocol.

\subsection{Participant preparation and procedural transparency}

A binding deadline should constrain the decision process rather than leave respondents uncertain about how the interface operates. In an online time-pressure experiment, Isler, Maule, and Starmer (2018) combined interface familiarization with advance explanations of the consequences of missing a deadline, achieving substantially higher compliance than earlier protocols. This evidence motivates preparation under the assigned condition: the five practice tasks reproduce the analytical task, and the timed instructions explain the countdown, automatic advancement, and preservation of any selection already made. In the timed condition, a brief comprehension check precedes practice and is repeated before the analytical sequence; incorrect answers receive explanatory feedback and may be corrected without disqualification.\footnote{The additional disclosures, comprehension checks, and nonresponse reminders are prospective procedural refinements. Previously collected responses retain their original procedural context and are not retrospectively treated as having received these additions.} The purpose is to establish understanding, not to screen respondents for decision speed. Br\"uhlmann et al. (2024) found that a passive warning did not reduce careless responding, while requiring participants to reproduce the warning increased attrition, which cautions against treating longer or more demanding warnings as an unqualified improvement.

Procedural clarity also requires respondents to know the consequences of nonresponse before investing time in the study. Agley, Mumaw, and Johnson (2024) recommend advance disclosure of rejection conditions, reminders at consent, and clear explanations when participation ends. Accordingly, the protocol specifies neutral advance disclosure that some respondents will face a nine-second deadline, without instructing the unconstrained groups to hurry. Consent explains the completion threshold, prohibited browser navigation, and the restriction of prize-draw registration to eligible completions. Timed respondents receive reminders after the first and second unanswered analytical choices; a third ends participation, with a reason-specific explanation and a research contact. Practice nonresponse does not count toward this threshold. These procedures distinguish a missed selection from dishonesty, but do not eliminate the possibility that the deadline changes who completes the study. Bouwmeester et al. (2017) documented substantial deadline noncompliance and differences between intention-to-treat and compliant-only estimates. We therefore retain incomplete records for recruitment accounting and interpret the substantive estimates as conditional on completion.

\begin{notes}
Linear probability models of candidate appearances, in percentage points, with standard errors clustered by respondent and candidate in parentheses. $M$: the candidate's description was opened; $Y$: the candidate was selected. Equation~\eqref{eq:lpm} is the main, preregistered model: its candidate-gender row is $\Gamma(B)$ and its interaction rows are $\Psi(z)$. In Equation~\eqref{eq:psi}, respondent effects absorb the condition indicators and candidate fixed effects absorb candidate gender, so only its interactions with \armT\ and \armC\ are estimated; Equation~\eqref{eq:gamma} drops candidate fixed effects to estimate the women-minus-men gap in each condition. Congruence compares the respondent's pretreatment self-placement with the candidate's displayed ideology. Respondent gender is centered. $R^2$ includes the fixed effects.
